title: Patterns Behind the Problem
description: Two original stories, two classic techniques. Start from the obvious solution, then find the pattern that makes it fast.

challenges.title: The Echo Protocol
story: You are building a communication protocol for a fleet of autonomous exploration robots.
To confirm a transmission arrived whole, the protocol looks for the same sequence of characters at the very start and the very end of the message: an opening signature and a closing signature.
The two signatures must sit in completely separate positions. They cannot share a single character. Find the longest signature possible.
challenges.statement: Given a string message, return the largest integer k such that the first k characters equal the last k characters and the two sequences do not overlap (2k ≤ length). Return 0 if no non-empty signature exists.

examples.why: Starts with "code" and ends with "code". They do not overlap.
Longer matches exist (3 and 4) but they overlap. "aa" … "aa" is the longest separate pair.
No non-empty prefix matches a suffix.

constraints: Lowercase English letters in the hidden tests; matching is case-sensitive.
The two signatures must not overlap.

hints.title: Understand the pattern
hints.text: You are looking for a piece of text that is both a prefix and a suffix of the same string. Ignore the overlap rule for a moment: what is the longest such piece? Then ask what happens to the answer when that piece is too long.

hints.title: Brute-force reasoning
hints.text: Try every length k from len(message) // 2 down to 1 and compare message[:k] with message[-k:]. The first match is the answer. It is correct, but each comparison costs up to k characters, so a string like "aaaa…ab" makes it O(n²).

hints.title: Optimisation
hints.text: Build the KMP "longest prefix that is also a suffix" (LPS) array in one pass. Its last entry is the longest border of the whole message. If that border is longer than half the message, lps[border - 1] gives the next shorter border. Keep following those links until the border fits.

reasoning.title: Explain it simply
reasoning.text: "I need the longest chunk that the message both starts and ends with, as long as the two copies do not touch."

reasoning.title: First idea
reasoning.text: Check every possible length from half the message downwards and compare the two slices directly. Stop at the first match.

reasoning.title: Why brute force is slow
reasoning.text: Each check re-reads up to n/2 characters from scratch and throws away what it learned. For long, repetitive messages that is about n²/4 character comparisons, which is billions at n = 100,000.

reasoning.title: Spot the pattern
reasoning.text: "Same text at the start and the end" is the definition of a border, and borders are exactly what the KMP prefix function computes. Whenever a problem talks about prefixes matching suffixes, repeated periods, or matching a pattern without restarting, think KMP.

reasoning.title: Say the optimisation out loud
reasoning.text: "The LPS array tells me, for every position, how much of the start I have already matched. On a mismatch I fall back to a shorter match I already know is valid, so I never re-compare characters from scratch. The pointer only moves forward n times and falls back at most that many times, so the whole build is linear. Then the borders of the full string form a chain: lps of the end, then lps of that, and so on. I walk the chain until the border fits in half the message."

reasoning.title: Complexity
reasoning.text: Time O(n): building the array is amortised linear and the fallback chain is at most n steps. Space O(n) for the LPS array.

challenges.whyFast: KMP avoids restarting: when the next character does not extend the current match, the LPS array already knows the next-longest prefix that still matches, so the scan continues from there instead of going back to the start. Every border of the whole message appears in the fallback chain from its last entry, so the longest non-overlapping one is found by following links, never by re-comparing text.
challenges.optimal:
def solution(message: str) -> int:
    length = len(message)
    # longest_border[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of message[:i + 1]
    # that is also a suffix of message[:i + 1]  (the KMP "LPS" array).
    longest_border = [0] * length
    matched = 0
    for position in range(1, length):
        # On a mismatch, fall back to the next shorter border instead of restarting.
        while matched > 0 and message[position] != message[matched]:
            matched = longest_border[matched - 1]
        if message[position] == message[matched]:
            matched += 1
        longest_border[position] = matched

    if length == 0:
        return 0
    # The longest border of the whole message may overlap itself.
    # Every shorter border is reachable by following the fallback links.
    candidate = longest_border[length - 1]
    while candidate > length // 2:
        candidate = longest_border[candidate - 1]
    return candidate
challenges.bruteComplexity: O(n²) time worst case, O(n) space for slices

challenges.title: The Mirror Vault
challenges.pattern: Prefix mirroring with a small candidate set
story: A high-security digital vault only accepts numeric access codes that read the same left to right and right to left.
When a code has to be replaced, the vault picks the numerically closest mirrored code. For security the replacement must differ from the old code, even if the old code is already mirrored.
If two replacements are equally close, the vault takes the smaller one. Write the replacement-code generator.
challenges.statement: Given a positive integer code, return the non-negative integer palindrome (no leading zeros, except 0 itself) that is different from code and has the smallest absolute difference from it. If two palindromes are equally close, return the smaller.

examples.why: 808 cannot be reused. 797 is 11 away and 818 is 10 away, so 818 wins.
The closest palindrome has fewer digits.
99 is already a palindrome but cannot be returned.
111 and 131 are both 10 away; the smaller wins.

constraints: No leading zeros. 0 is a valid replacement.

hints.title: Understand the pattern
hints.text: A palindrome is completely decided by its left half. Look at how close 12921 is to 12345 compared with 99999. Which digits of a number matter most when you are trying to stay close to it?

hints.title: Brute-force reasoning
hints.text: Step outwards: check code - 1, code + 1, code - 2, code + 2 … and return the first palindrome. Checking the lower side first handles ties. It is correct, but near 10^18 the gap between palindromes can be around 10^9, far too many steps.

hints.title: Optimisation
hints.text: Take the left half (including the middle digit for odd lengths). Mirror it, and mirror it after adding or subtracting 1. Also add the two digit-boundary codes 99…9 (one digit shorter) and 10…01 (one digit longer). Drop the original code and pick the closest, smaller on ties.

reasoning.title: Explain it simply
reasoning.text: "Find the nearest number that reads the same both ways, but not the number itself, and prefer the smaller one on a tie."

reasoning.title: First idea
reasoning.text: Walk outwards from the code one step at a time and test each number for being a palindrome.

reasoning.title: Why brute force is slow
reasoning.text: The number of steps equals the distance to the answer, which can be about the square root of the code. For 18-digit codes that is up to a billion checks.

reasoning.title: Spot the pattern
reasoning.text: When the answer must be "the nearest value with some structure" and the structure is fixed by a small part of the input (here, the left half), generate the few candidates that structure allows instead of searching. Keeping the left half as close as possible keeps the high-value digits unchanged.

reasoning.title: Say the optimisation out loud
reasoning.text: "The left half decides everything, and the most significant digits matter most, so the answer's left half is the current one, one more, or one less. Mirroring those gives three candidates. The only time the length changes is around 99…9 and 10…01, so I add those two. Five candidates, remove the original, pick the closest, smaller on ties."

reasoning.title: Complexity
reasoning.text: Time O(d) with d decimal digits: a constant number of candidates, each built and compared in O(d). Space O(d) for the strings.

challenges.whyFast: Any palindrome with the same digit count is fixed by its left half, and changing that half by more than 1 moves the result further away than changing it by 1. So prefix − 1, prefix and prefix + 1 cover every same-length winner. The only other possibilities have a different number of digits, and the closest of those are always 99…9 just below and 10…01 just above, which is why the two boundary candidates are needed (1000 → 999, 99 → 101).
challenges.bruteComplexity: O(√code · d) time in the worst case, O(d) space

tests.label: Single digit
tests.why: 0 and 2 tie at distance 1; 0 is smaller.

tests.label: Very large
tests.why: Only five candidates are ever needed.
